common_name: White Waves Toad Lily (Creamy White-Centered Variegated Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'White Waves' arose as a sport of the variegated cultivar 'Imperial Banner' and shows a broader, more solid creamy-white leaf center.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting the plant where its pale foliage center will show against darker-leaved companions. 'White Waves' arose as a sport of the variegated cultivar 'Imperial Banner' and carries a broader, more solid creamy-white leaf center bordered by a clean green margin, lacking the fine green streaking found in its parent. Clumps stay compact at around 15 inches tall and are topped in early fall with purple-spotted, orchid-like flowers typical of the toad lily group. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter; some gentle morning sun helps hold the crisp white variegation without scorching the leaf pattern.

common_name: Raspberry Mousse Toad Lily (Heavily Speckled Red-Purple Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; 'Raspberry Mousse' is valued for flowers so densely overlaid with dark reddish-purple speckling that the blooms read as nearly solid red-purple.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, giving the arching stems room to display flowers along their full length. 'Raspberry Mousse' is notable among toad lily cultivars for blooms so heavily overlaid with dark reddish-purple speckling that they read as a nearly solid red-purple rather than the spotted pattern typical of the genus. Upright stems reach roughly 18 to 24 inches and open their richly colored, orchid-like flowers from late summer into early fall, extending color into the shade garden's slower season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering density.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden — Tricyrtis Plant Evaluation

common_name: Cedric Bassett Jade Lily (Heavy-Flowering Fragrant Reineckea)

planting.note: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring or plant container-grown starts into moist, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; 'Cedric Bassett' is a selection named for the plantsman who found it, prized for flowering far more heavily than the typical species.

directions: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring or plant container-grown starts into moist, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; 'Cedric Bassett' is a selection prized for flowering far more heavily than the typical species. Low spikes of fragrant, lavender-pink flowers open at the base of the glossy, strap-like foliage in autumn, making this form a better choice than plain jade lily where a strong fragrant bloom display is the goal rather than just the evergreen groundcover effect. Growth habit, rhizome spread, and foliage otherwise match the species, eventually forming a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen carpet in deep shade. Allow new plantings a full season to establish before expecting significant flowering.

common_name: Jinfo Jewel Jade Lily (Dwarf Mountain-Collected Reineckea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to part shade; 'Jinfo Jewel' is a distinctly dwarf form collected from moss-covered limestone outcrops atop Jinfo Mountain in China.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to part shade; 'Jinfo Jewel' is a distinctly dwarf form collected from moss-covered limestone outcrops atop Jinfo Mountain in China, reaching only a few inches tall compared with the taller typical species. Because the foliage stays so short, the fragrant pink-and-white autumn flowers sit well above the leaf canopy and are far more visible than the mostly hidden blooms of standard jade lily. Its tight, low habit and slow rhizome spread make it well suited to shaded rock garden pockets, trough plantings, or the front edge of a woodland bed where a taller groundcover would overwhelm the scale. Give it the same humus-rich, evenly moist deep-shade conditions as the species, dividing clumps in spring if increase is desired.
